4                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                       
5                     NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                     
6                            SAN JOSE DIVISION                            
7                                                                         
8    UNILOC USA, INC., et al.,        Case No.  19-cv-01692-EJD (VKD)     

9              Plaintiffs,                                                
                                      ORDER RE DISCOVERY DISPUTE RE       
10          v.                         APPLE DOCUMENT SUBPOENA TO          
                                      PENDRELL                            
11    APPLE INC.,                                                          
                                      Re: Dkt. No. 168                    
               Defendants.                                                
12                                                                         

13                                                                         
14        Defendant Apple Inc. (“Apple”) and non-party Pendrell Technologies, LLC (“Pendrell”) 
15   have filed a joint discovery dispute letter concerning Apple’s document subpoena to Pendrell.  
16   Dkt. No. 168.  Apple asks for an order compelling Pendrell to produce documents responsive to 
17   the subpoena and to prepare a privilege log.  Pendrell objects that this Court has no authority to 
18   enforce Apple’s subpoena because Pendrell is a non-party located in the state of Washington, 
19   beyond this Court’s jurisdiction.  In the alternative, Pendrell objects to Apple’s request on the 
20   merits and seeks a protective order.  The Court deems this matter suitable for resolution without a 
21   hearing.  Civil L.R. 7-1(b).                                          
22        For the reasons explained below, the Court finds it has authority to consider the dispute but 
23   denies Apple’s request for relief.                                    
24   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
25        Apple served the subpoena at issue on Pendrell on January 27, 2020.  Dkt. No. 168 at ECF 
26   p. 1, 5; see Dkt. No. 168-1.1  The subpoena reflects that Pendrell is located in Kirkland, 
27                                                                         
1   Washington, but the document production portion of the subpoena specifies a place of production 
2   in San Francisco, California.  Dkt. No. 168-1 at ECF p. 5.  It is not clear whether Pendrell served 
3   any objections to this subpoena.  Pendrell attaches to the discovery dispute letter written 
4   “responses” that appear to correspond to the document requests in Apple’s subpoena, but these 
5   responses are undated, and by Pendrell’s own account, they were served in response to other, 
6   similar Apple subpoenas served in other cases.  See Dkt. No. 168-2; Dkt. No. 168 at ECF p. 4 
7   (referring to a response served on October 10, 2019, before the date of the subpoena at issue, 
8   regarding Apple subpoenas served in Case Nos. 19-cv-1697-VC, 19-cv-1904-WHO, and 19-cv-
9   1929-EJD).  In any event, these responses do not include any objection to the place of production 
10   of documents.  Pendrell says that it never agreed to produce responsive documents in San 
11   Francisco, California.2  Dkt. No. 168 at ECF p. 5.                    
12   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
13        A.   Jurisdiction                                                
14        Subpoena-related motions under Rule 45 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure must be 
15   filed in “the court for the district where compliance is required.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(d)(2)(B)(i), 
16   (d)(3)(A), (d)(3)(B), (e)(2)(B).  Here, Apple’s subpoena specifies a place of compliance in San 
17   Francisco, California.  Pendrell objects that the subpoena does not comply with the geographic 
18   limits on the place of compliance specified in Rule 45(c) and for this reason the Court lacks 
19   jurisdiction to decide the dispute.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(c)(2)(A) (the place of compliance for a 
20   subpoena commanding the production of documents must be “within 100 miles of where the 
21   person resides, is employed, or regularly transacts business in person”). 
22        Although there is disagreement among the federal district courts on this point,3 the Court 
23   concludes that under the plain language of Rule 45(d), Apple’s motion to compel is properly filed 
24                                                                         

25                                                                         
    on January 27, 2020.                                                  

26                                                                         
    2 Pendrell asserts that all of Apple’s other document subpoenas have specified Seattle, Washington 
    as the place of compliance.  Dkt. No. 168 at ECF p. 4.                
27                                                                         
1   in this district, as it is the place where compliance is required on the face of the subpoena, even if 
2   that place of compliance is not proper under Rule 45(c).  Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(d)(2)(B)(i); see, e.g., 
3   CSS, Inc. v. Herrington, 354 F. Supp. 3d 702, 709 (N.D. Tex. 2017) (“for purposes of a Rule 
4   45(d)(2) or 45(d)(3) motion, the court or district ‘where compliance is required’ is determined by 
5   the location or ‘place’ for compliance identified on the subpoena”); but see, e.g., Raap v. Brier & 
6   Thorn, Inc., No. 17-MC-3001, 2017 WL 2462823, at *2-3 (C.D. Ill. July 7, 2017) (place where 
7   compliance is required is the location required by Rule 45(c)).       
8        B.   Apple’s Request for Relief                                  
9        Apple seeks to enforce its document subpoena against Pendrell.  It asks for an order 
10   requiring Pendrell to search an archive containing more than 550,000 files.  Apple also asks for an 
11   order requiring Pendrell to prepare a privilege log for any claims of privilege pertaining to non-
12   email documents.  Dkt. No. 168 at ECF p. 1-3.  Pendrell objects that Apple’s request is unduly 
13   burdensome and disproportionate to the needs of the case.  Pendrell also objects that Apple 
14   unreasonably delayed until the very end of the discovery period to make its extraordinary demand, 
15   particularly when the issues could have been raised earlier in the discovery period.  Id. at ECF 
16   p. 6-8.                                                               
17        The Court denies Apple’s motion on three grounds.  First, the Court declines to enforce a 
18   subpoena that clearly does not comply with Rule 45(c).  “Although Rule 45(a)(1)(A)(iii) permits 
19   the subpoena to direct a place of compliance, that place must be selected under Rule 45(c).”  Fed. 
20   R. Civ. P. 45 advisory committee’s note to 2013 amendment, Subdivision (c).  While nothing in 
21   Rule 45(c) prevents parties from arranging to produce documents by electronic means rather than 
22   at a physical location, a subpoena that purports to compel production beyond the geographical 
23   limits specified in Rule 45(c) does not comply with the requirements of the Rule.  See id; Fed. R. 
24   Civ. P. 45(d)(3)(A).  Apple points out that Pendrell did not object to San Francisco, California as 
25   the place of compliance.  That may be, but while a non-party may voluntarily produce documents 
26   at a location more than 100 miles from its place of business, Apple cites no authority for the 
27   proposition that the Court must construe such voluntary production as consent or waiver when the 
    1    objections in opposition to a motion to compel. 
    2          Second, the Court is not persuaded that the archived files Apple asks Pendrell to search are 
    3  ||  likely to contain non-privileged materials that are relevant to a claim or defense.  Apple describes 
    4  ||  the materials as an “additional data source” that Pendrell disclosed in September 2020 that may 
    5    contain information about valuations of a large patent portfolio that includes the asserted patent. 
    6  || Dkt. No. 168 at ECF p. 1.  Pendrell describes the materials as “internal, litigation-focused 
    7    documents—generated for and at the direction of attorneys for potential litigation—from 
    8    Pendrell’s Ovidian division between 2012 and 2018.”  Id. at ECF p. 6.  Apart from referring to the 
    9  || Court’s order resolving a prior discovery dispute, Apple’s portion of the discovery dispute letter 
   10  ||  does little to explain why it believes these materials contain relevant and responsive documents 
   11    and why it believes the very significant effort that would be required to review the archived files 
    12  ||  for responsive documents is justified here. 
5    13          Third, from the record before the Court it appears that Apple did not timely confer with 
    14  || Pendrell about this discovery dispute in a manner that would have permitted the parties to attempt 
 3    15    in good faith to resolve their disagreements without seeking the Court’s assistance.  Pendrell is not 
     16    a party, and Apple must take reasonable steps to avoid imposing undue burden and expense on a 
 3    17    non-party who is subject to a subpoena, even if the non-party is represented by the same counsel 
    18  || representing Uniloc.  Fed. R. Civ. 45(d).  Apple has not taken these steps, nor does it appear to 
   19  || have complied with the letter and spirit of the Court’s Standing Order regarding discovery dispute 
   20 || resolution. 
   21  || I.    CONCLUSION 
   22          The Court denies Apple’s request for an order compelling production of documents and 
   23    preparation of a privilege log. 
   24          IT IS SO ORDERED. 
   25    Dated: October 23, 2020 

                                                         VIRGINIA K. DEMARCH 
                                                        United States Magistrate Judge 
   28
